properties.headline: Air Quality Alert issued August 31 at 6:17PM CDT by NWS Kansas City/Pleasant Hill MO
properties.description:
The Mid-America Regional Council has issued a code Orange Air
Quality Alert for the Kansas City metropolitan area, with ground
level ozone being the primary pollutant from 9 AM to 7 PM CDT
Tuesday.

Members of sensitive groups may experience health effects.

People and businesses are urged to avoid activities which lead to
ozone formation. These activities include refueling vehicles or
topping off when refueling idling vehicles unnecessarily and using
gasoline powered lawn equipment. Positive activities include car
pooling, biking to work, delaying or combining errands, and using
water-based paints and cleaners.

When pollution levels are elevated, the Mid-America Regional Council
recommends that individuals consider limiting strenuous outdoor
physical activity to reduce the risk of adverse health effects.
People who may be especially sensitive to the effects of elevated
levels of pollutants include the very young and those with
preexisting respiratory problems such as asthma or heart disease.
Those with symptoms should consider consulting their personal
physician.

For further information, please see the Mid-America Regional Council
air quality program website at http://www.airqkc.org.
properties.note: Non-Weather Emergency Message. Not sent to IPAWS.

NWSheadline: AIR QUALITY ALERT IN EFFECT FROM 9 AM TO 7 PM CDT TUESDAY

miles and take hours to reach your location from upstream rain areas.

properties.headline: Tropical Cyclone Local Statement issued August 31 at 5:08PM CDT by NWS Lake Charles LA
properties.description:
HLSLCH

This product covers Southwest Louisiana and Southeast Texas

**TROPICAL STORM WARNING ISSUED FOR PORTIONS OF THE UPPER TEXAS AND
SOUTHWESTERN LOUISIANA COAST**


NEW INFORMATION
---------------

* CHANGES TO WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- A Tropical Storm Warning has been issued for Lower Vermilion
- A Storm Surge Watch has been issued for East Cameron, Lower
Jefferson, and West Cameron

* CURRENT WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- A Tropical Storm Warning is in effect for Lower Vermilion
- A Tropical Storm Warning and Storm Surge Watch are in effect
for East Cameron, Lower Jefferson, and West Cameron

* STORM INFORMATION:
- About 170 miles southeast of Sabine Pass TX or about 150 miles
southeast of Cameron LA
- 28.2N 91.5W
- Storm Intensity 35 mph
- Movement West-northwest or 300 degrees at 6 mph

SITUATION OVERVIEW
------------------

Tropical Depression Five is located about 100 miles south of Morgan
City moving WNW at 6MPH. A west-northwestward to northwestward motion
is forecast during the next couple of days. On the forecast track, the
center of the system is predicted to reach the northwestern Gulf Coast
within the warning area on Tuesday and move inland over southeast Texas
on Tuesday night.

Maximum sustained winds are near 35 mph (55 km/h) with higher gusts.
Strengthening is expected, and the depression is likely to become a
tropical storm this evening.

The estimated minimum central pressure is 1011 mb (29.86 inches).



POTENTIAL IMPACTS
-----------------

* FLOODING RAIN:
Protect against dangerous rainfall flooding having possible
significant impacts across SETX. Potential impacts include:
- Moderate rainfall flooding may prompt several evacuations and
rescues.
- Rivers and tributaries may quickly become swollen with swifter
currents and overspill their banks in a few places, especially
in usually vulnerable spots. Small streams, creeks, canals, and
ditches overflow.
- Flood waters can enter some structures or weaken foundations.
Several places may experience expanded areas of rapid
inundation at underpasses, low-lying spots, and poor drainage
areas. Some streets and parking lots take on moving water as
storm drains and retention ponds overflow. Driving conditions
become hazardous. Some road and bridge closures.

Protect against locally hazardous rainfall flooding having possible
limited impacts across SWLA.

* SURGE:
Protect against life-threatening surge having possible significant
impacts across Coastal Southeast Texas and Southwest Louisiana.
Potential impacts in this area include:
- Areas of inundation with storm surge flooding accentuated by
waves. Damage to several buildings, mainly near the coast.
- Sections of near-shore escape routes and secondary roads become
weakened or washed out, especially in usually vulnerable low
spots.
- Major beach erosion with heavy surf breaching dunes. Strong and
numerous rip currents.
- Moderate damage to marinas, docks, boardwalks, and piers.
Several small craft broken away from moorings, especially in
unprotected anchorages.

Also, protect against locally hazardous surge having possible limited
impacts across lower Vermilion Parish.

Elsewhere across Southwest Louisiana and Southeast Texas, little to
no impact is anticipated.

* WIND:
Protect against hazardous wind having possible limited impacts across
Southeast Texas and Southwest Louisiana. Potential impacts in this area
include:
- Damage to porches, awnings, carports, sheds, and unanchored
mobile homes. Unsecured lightweight objects blown about.
- Many large tree limbs broken off. A few trees snapped or
uprooted, but with greater numbers in places where trees are
shallow rooted. Some fences and roadway signs blown over.
- A few roads impassable from debris, particularly within urban
or heavily wooded places. Hazardous driving conditions on
bridges and other elevated roadways.
- Scattered power and communications outages.

Elsewhere across Southwest Louisiana and Southeast Texas, little to
no impact is anticipated.

PRECAUTIONARY/PREPAREDNESS ACTIONS
----------------------------------

* EVACUATIONS:
Follow the advice of local officials.

* OTHER PREPAREDNESS INFORMATION:

Keep cell phones well charged. Cell phone chargers for automobiles
can be helpful, but be aware of your risk for deadly carbon monoxide
poisoning if your car is left idling in a garage or other poorly
ventilated area.

If you are a visitor, be sure to know the name of the city or town in
which you are staying and the name of the county or parish in which
it resides. Listen for these locations in local news updates. Pay
attention for instructions from local authorities.

Closely monitor weather.gov, NOAA Weather radio or local news outlets
for official storm information. Be ready to adapt to possible changes
to the forecast. Ensure you have multiple ways to receive weather
warnings.

* ADDITIONAL SOURCES OF INFORMATION:
- For information on appropriate preparations see ready.gov
- For information on creating an emergency plan see getagameplan.org
- For additional disaster preparedness information see redcross.org

NEXT UPDATE
-----------

The next local statement will be issued by the National Weather
Service in Lake Charles LA around 11 PM CDT, or sooner if conditions
warrant.

Springdale...elevated river levels are forecast.

* WHERE...Virgin River at Virgin.

* WHEN...From this afternoon to late tonight.

developed areas near the town of Virgin.

6 PM and remain elevated through tonight.

properties.headline: Tropical Cyclone Local Statement issued August 31 at 4:33PM CDT by NWS Houston/Galveston TX
properties.description:
HLSHGX

This product covers Southeast Texas

**Tropical Depression Five to Bring Locally Heavy Rainfall for
Portions of Southeast Texas**


NEW INFORMATION
---------------

* CHANGES TO WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- None

* CURRENT WATCHES AND WARNINGS:
- A Tropical Storm Warning is in effect for Bolivar Peninsula and
Chambers

* STORM INFORMATION:
- About 210 miles east-southeast of Galveston TX
- 28.2N 91.5W
- Storm Intensity 35 mph
- Movement West-northwest or 300 degrees at 6 mph

SITUATION OVERVIEW
------------------

Tropical Depression Five is currently about 105 miles south of the
Louisiana coast, slowly moving west-northwestward towards the
northwestern Gulf Coast. It is expected to become a Tropical Storm
within the next 24 hours, before making landfall along the Upper Texas
coast, somewhere within the Warning area. Periods of moderate to heavy
rainfall associated are expected to begin as early as late tonight and
lasting into late Tuesday night/early Wednesday morning. 3-5 inches of
rain with isolated amounts of 6-9 inches are expected with the highest
totals occuring east of I-45. Rainfall rates will exceed 3-4 inches
per hour at times in the heaviest downpours, which can lead to flash
flooding especially in urban and vulnerable areas.

POTENTIAL IMPACTS
-----------------

* FLOODING RAIN:
Protect against dangerous rainfall flooding having possible
significant impacts mainly for areas east of I-45. Potential
impacts include:
- Moderate rainfall flooding may prompt several evacuations and
rescues.
- Rivers and tributaries may quickly become swollen with swifter
currents and overspill their banks in a few places, especially
in usually vulnerable spots. Small streams, creeks, canals, and
ditches overflow.
- Flood waters can enter some structures or weaken foundations.
Several places may experience expanded areas of rapid
inundation at underpasses, low-lying spots, and poor drainage
areas. Some streets and parking lots take on moving water as
storm drains and retention ponds overflow. Driving conditions
become hazardous. Some road and bridge closures.

Protect against locally hazardous rainfall flooding having possible
limited impacts across the rest of Southeast Texas.

* WIND:
Protect against hazardous wind having possible limited impacts across
Bolivar Peninsula and Chambers County
. Potential impacts in this area include:
- Damage to porches, awnings, carports, sheds, and unanchored
mobile homes. Unsecured lightweight objects blown about.
- Many large tree limbs broken off. A few trees snapped or
uprooted, but with greater numbers in places where trees are
shallow rooted. Some fences and roadway signs blown over.
- A few roads impassable from debris, particularly within urban
or heavily wooded places. Hazardous driving conditions on
bridges and other elevated roadways.
- Scattered power and communications outages.

Elsewhere across Southeast Texas, little to no impact is anticipated.

* SURGE:
Protect against locally hazardous surge having possible limited
impacts across Port Bolivar to High Island. Potential impacts in
this area include:
- Localized inundation with storm surge flooding mainly along
immediate shorelines and in low-lying spots, or in areas
farther inland near where higher surge waters move ashore.
- Sections of near-shore roads and parking lots become overspread
with surge water. Driving conditions dangerous in places where
surge water covers the road.
- Moderate beach erosion. Heavy surf also breaching dunes, mainly
in usually vulnerable locations. Strong rip currents.
- Minor to locally moderate damage to marinas, docks, boardwalks,
and piers. A few small craft broken away from moorings.

Elsewhere across Southeast Texas, little to no impact is anticipated.

* TORNADOES:
Little to no impacts are anticipated at this time
across Southeast Texas.

PRECAUTIONARY/PREPAREDNESS ACTIONS
----------------------------------

* EVACUATIONS:
Follow the advice of local officials.


* OTHER PREPAREDNESS INFORMATION:
Now is the time to complete all preparations to protect life and
property in accordance with your emergency plan. Ensure you are in a
safe location before the onset of strong winds or possible flooding.

Keep cell phones well charged. Cell phone chargers for automobiles
can be helpful, but be aware of your risk for deadly carbon monoxide
poisoning if your car is left idling in a garage or other poorly
ventilated area.

If you are a visitor, be sure to know the name of the city or town in
which you are staying and the name of the county or parish in which
it resides. Listen for these locations in local news updates. Pay
attention for instructions from local authorities.

Closely monitor weather.gov, NOAA Weather radio or local news outlets
for official storm information. Be ready to adapt to possible changes
to the forecast. Ensure you have multiple ways to receive weather
warnings.


* ADDITIONAL SOURCES OF INFORMATION:
- For information on appropriate preparations see ready.gov
- For information on creating an emergency plan see getagameplan.org
- For additional disaster preparedness information see redcross.org

NEXT UPDATE
-----------

The next local statement will be issued by the National Weather
Service in Houston/Galveston TX around , or sooner if conditions
warrant.

an Ozone Action Day for the Dallas-Fort Worth area for Tuesday,
September 1, 2026.

avoiding drive-through lanes, conserving energy, and keeping your

Take extra precautions when outside. Wear lightweight and loose
fitting clothing. Try to limit strenuous activities to early morning
or evening. Take action when you see symptoms of heat exhaustion and

Health Administration recommends scheduling frequent rest breaks in
shaded or air conditioned environments. Anyone overcome by heat
should be moved to a cool and shaded location. Heat stroke is an
emergency! Call 9 1 1.

interiors will reach lethal temperatures in a matter of minutes.

properties.headline: Red Flag Warning issued August 31 at 12:30PM PDT until August 31 at 8:00PM PDT by NWS Medford OR
properties.description:
* AFFECTED AREA...In California...Scott Valley in Fire Weather
Zone 280, Fire Weather Zone 281, Fire Weather Zone 284 except
the southeast portion of this zone, and Fire Weather Zone 285.
In Oregon...Fire Weather Zone 624, except the Highway 97
corridor from Modoc Point to Chemult.

* WIND...South winds 10 to 20 mph with gusts to 30 mph in the
Scott Valley, and 15 to 25 mph with gusts to 35 mph in the
Shasta Valley. Elsewhere, southwest winds 10 to 20 mph with
gusts to 30 mph.

* HUMIDITY...Minimum humidity 9 to 15 percent.

* DETAILED URL...View the hazard area in detail at
https://weather.gov/wrh/hazards?wfo=mfr
properties.instruction:
Follow all fire restrictions. You can find your county's
emergency sign up form as well as links to fire restrictions at
weather.gov/medford/wildfire. One less spark, one less wildfire.

Be sure you're signed up for your county's emergency alert
system. Familiarize yourself with your emergency plan and make
sure you listen to emergency services. Visit ready.gov/plan for
more information.

A Red Flag Warning is issued when we identify weather conditions
that promote rapid spread of fire which may become life-
threatening. This does not mean there is a fire. These conditions
are either occurring now or will begin soon. It is important to
have multiple ways to receive information from authorities.

NWSheadline: RED FLAG WARNING REMAINS IN EFFECT UNTIL 8 PM PDT THIS EVENING FOR STRONG GUSTY WIND AND LOW RH FOR FIRE WEATHER ZONES 280, 281, 284, 285, AND 624

properties.areaDesc: Madison; St. Clair; Monroe; St. Charles; St. Louis; St. Louis City; Jefferson
properties.headline: Heat Advisory issued August 31 at 2:29PM CDT until September 4 at 8:00PM CDT by NWS St Louis MO
properties.description:
* WHAT...Heat index values up to 108.

* WHERE...In Illinois, Madison IL, Monroe IL, and Saint Clair IL
Counties. In Missouri, Jefferson MO, Saint Charles MO, Saint Louis
City MO, and Saint Louis MO Counties.

* WHEN...Until 8 PM CDT Friday.

* IMPACTS...Hot temperatures and high humidity may cause heat
illnesses.
properties.instruction:
Drink plenty of fluids, stay in an air-conditioned room, stay out of
the sun, and check up on relatives and neighbors. Young children and
pets should never be left unattended in vehicles under any
circumstances. Take extra precautions if you work or spend time
outside. When possible reschedule strenuous activities to early
morning or evening. Know the signs and symptoms of heat exhaustion
and heat stroke. Wear lightweight and loose fitting clothing when
possible. To reduce risk during outdoor work, the Occupational Safety
and Health Administration recommends scheduling frequent rest breaks
in shaded or air conditioned environments. Anyone overcome by heat
should be moved to a cool and shaded location. Heat stroke is an
emergency! Call 9 1 1.

People in the Saint Louis Metropolitan Area can get information about
cooling centers or energy assistance related to the excessive heat by
calling the United Way of Greater Saint Louis at 800-427-4626, or if
calling from a land line phone dial 2-1-1. You can also call Cool
Down Saint Louis at 314-241-7668.

NWSheadline: HEAT ADVISORY REMAINS IN EFFECT UNTIL 8 PM CDT FRIDAY

properties.areaDesc: Kittitas, WA
properties.headline: Air Quality Alert issued August 31 at 12:07PM PDT by NWS Pendleton OR
properties.description:
The Washington State Department of Ecology has issued an Air Quality
Alert until 10 AM PDT Wednesday.

An Air Quality Alert has been issued for Kittitas County through
Wednesday Sept 2 at 10AM due to current and expected wildfire smoke
from regional fires. Particulate matter (PM2.5) may reach Unhealthy
to Sensitive Groups to Unhealthy levels for areas directly downwind
from active fires, especially overnight and during the early morning
hours. Be sure to check air monitors in your area before outdoor
activities. When air quality is Unhealthy, everyone should reduce
exposure. Limit time outside, avoid, strenuous outdoor activity, and
follow tips for cleaner indoor air.

Information from the Washington Department of Ecology web site is
available at http://www.ecy.wa.gov/air.html or call 360-407-6000.
properties.note: Non-Weather Emergency Message. Not sent to IPAWS.

NWSheadline: AIR QUALITY ALERT IN EFFECT UNTIL 10 AM PDT WEDNESDAY

properties.areaDesc: Crook, OR; Deschutes, OR; Jefferson, OR; Wasco, OR
properties.headline: Air Quality Alert issued August 31 at 12:07PM PDT by NWS Pendleton OR
properties.description:
Oregon Department of Environmental Quality has issued an Air Quality
Advisory until noon PDT Wednesday.

For the Smoke Air Quality Advisory, wildfires burning in the region
combined with forecasted conditions will cause air quality to reach
unhealthy levels.

Pollutants in smoke can cause burning eyes, runny nose, aggravate
heart and lung diseases, and aggravate other serious health
problems.  Limit outdoor activities and keep children indoors if it
is smoky. Please follow medical advice if you have a heart or lung
condition.

For additional information...please visit the Web site at
http://www.oregon.gov/DEQ
properties.note: Non-Weather Emergency Message. Not sent to IPAWS.

properties.headline: Flood Watch issued August 31 at 11:51AM MST until August 31 at 8:00PM MST by NWS Phoenix AZ
properties.description:
The environment will remain conducive for additional showers and
thunderstorms through early this evening, mainly across La Paz,
northern Yuma and western Maricopa Counties. Training of storms could
lead to an additional 1 to 2 inches of rainfall causing rapid run-off
and flooding of low-water crossings and low-lying areas.

* WHAT...Flooding caused by excessive rainfall continues to be
possible.

* WHERE...A portion of south central Arizona, including the following
areas, Aguila Valley, Sonoran Desert Natl Monument and Tonopah
Desert.

* WHEN...Until 8 PM MST this evening.

* IMPACTS...Excessive runoff may result in flooding of rivers,
creeks, streams, and other low-lying and flood-prone locations.

* ADDITIONAL DETAILS...
- Another round of showers and thunderstorms is likely during the
afternoon and evening hours. Heavy rainfall will be possible
which may cause localized flooding.
- http://www.weather.gov/safety/flood
properties.instruction:

Warnings. Those living in areas prone to flooding should be prepared
to take action should flooding develop.

properties.description:
The National Weather Service in Reno has issued a Red Flag
Warning for gusty winds and low humidity, which is in effect from
11 AM to 11 PM PDT Tuesday. The Fire Weather Watch is no longer
in effect.

* CHANGES...The Fire Weather Watch has been upgraded to a Red Flag
Warning.

* Affected Area...Fire Weather Zone 270 Surprise Valley
California, Fire Weather Zone 278 Eastern Lassen County, Fire
Weather Zone 458 Northern Washoe County, including the S-1 Vya
Fire.

* Winds...Southwest 15 to 25 mph with gusts of 30 to 40 mph.
Ridgetop gusts up to 45 mph. Winds shift to westerly in the
late afternoon and evening.

* Humidity...RH reductions to 12 to 17 percent in the afternoon.
Nighttime recoveries of 50 to 80 percent Wednesday morning.

* Duration...3 to 6 hours.

* Impacts...The combination of gusty winds and low humidity can
cause fire to rapidly grow in size and intensity before first
responders can contain them.
properties.instruction:
Avoid outdoor activities that can cause a spark near dry
vegetation, such as yard work, target shooting, or campfires.
Follow local fire restrictions. Check weather.gov/reno for
updates and livingwithfire.info for preparedness tips.

properties.description:
The Oregon Department of Environmental Quality has issued an Air
Quality Advisory, which is IN EFFECT UNTIL NOON PDT WEDNESDAY for
eastern Marion County.

An Air Quality Advisory for Smoke has been issued for eastern Marion
County. Wildfires burning in the region combined with forecasted
conditions will cause air quality to reach unhealthy levels at times
through noon Wednesday.

Pollutants in smoke can cause burning eyes, runny nose, aggravate
heart and lung diseases, and aggravate other serious health
problems. Limit outdoor activities and keep children indoors if it
is smoky. Please follow medical advice if you have a heart or lung
condition.

More information about air quality can be found at:
www.orcaa.org
www.swcleanair.gov
www.oregon.gov/DEQ
www.lrapa.org

- A Tropical Storm Warning is in effect for Bolivar Peninsula and
Chambers

* STORM INFORMATION:
- About 260 miles east-southeast of Galveston TX
- 28.0N 90.8W
- Storm Intensity 35 mph
- Movement West-northwest or 285 degrees at 5 mph

SITUATION OVERVIEW
------------------

Tropical Depression Five is currently about 120 miles south of the
Louisiana coast, slowly moving west-northwestward towards the
northwestern Gulf Coast. It is expected to become a Tropical Storm
within the next 24 hours or so, before making landfall along the
Upper Texas coast, somewhere within the Warning area. Periods of
moderate to heavy rainfall associated are expected to begin as early
as late tonight and lasting into late Tuesday night/early Wednesday
morning. 3-5 inches of rain with isolated amounts of 6-9 inches are
expected with the highest totals occuring east of I-45. Rainfall
rates will exceed 3-4 inches per hour at times in the heaviest
downpours, which can lead to flash flooding especially in urban and
vulnerable areas.

POTENTIAL IMPACTS
-----------------

* FLOODING RAIN:
Protect against dangerous rainfall flooding having possible
significant impacts across mainly for areas east of I-45. Potential
impacts include:
- Moderate rainfall flooding may prompt several evacuations and
rescues.
- Rivers and tributaries may quickly become swollen with swifter
currents and overspill their banks in a few places, especially
in usually vulnerable spots. Small streams, creeks, canals, and
ditches overflow.
- Flood waters can enter some structures or weaken foundations.
Several places may experience expanded areas of rapid
inundation at underpasses, low-lying spots, and poor drainage
areas. Some streets and parking lots take on moving water as
storm drains and retention ponds overflow. Driving conditions
become hazardous. Some road and bridge closures.

Protect against locally hazardous rainfall flooding having possible
limited impacts across across the rest of Southeast Texas..

* WIND:
Protect against hazardous wind having possible limited impacts across
Bolivar Peninsula and Chambers County. Potential impacts in this area include:
- Damage to porches, awnings, carports, sheds, and unanchored
mobile homes. Unsecured lightweight objects blown about.
- Many large tree limbs broken off. A few trees snapped or
uprooted, but with greater numbers in places where trees are
shallow rooted. Some fences and roadway signs blown over.
- A few roads impassable from debris, particularly within urban
or heavily wooded places. Hazardous driving conditions on
bridges and other elevated roadways.
- Scattered power and communications outages.

Elsewhere across Southeast Texas, little to no impact is anticipated.

* SURGE:
Protect against locally hazardous surge having possible limited
impacts across Port Bolivar to High Island. Potential impacts in
this area include:
- Localized inundation with storm surge flooding mainly along
immediate shorelines and in low-lying spots, or in areas
farther inland near where higher surge waters move ashore.
- Sections of near-shore roads and parking lots become overspread
with surge water. Driving conditions dangerous in places where
surge water covers the road.
- Moderate beach erosion. Heavy surf also breaching dunes, mainly
in usually vulnerable locations. Strong rip currents.
- Minor to locally moderate damage to marinas, docks, boardwalks,
and piers. A few small craft broken away from moorings.

Elsewhere across Southeast Texas, little to no impact is anticipated.

* TORNADOES:
Little to no impacts are anticipated at this time
across Southeast Texas.

PRECAUTIONARY/PREPAREDNESS ACTIONS
----------------------------------

* EVACUATIONS:
Follow the advice of local officials.


* OTHER PREPAREDNESS INFORMATION:
Now is the time to complete all preparations to protect life and
property in accordance with your emergency plan. Ensure you are in a
safe location before the onset of strong winds or possible flooding.

Keep cell phones well charged. Cell phone chargers for automobiles
can be helpful, but be aware of your risk for deadly carbon monoxide
poisoning if your car is left idling in a garage or other poorly
ventilated area.

If you are a visitor, be sure to know the name of the city or town in
which you are staying and the name of the county or parish in which
it resides. Listen for these locations in local news updates. Pay
attention for instructions from local authorities.

Closely monitor weather.gov, NOAA Weather radio or local news outlets
for official storm information. Be ready to adapt to possible changes
to the forecast. Ensure you have multiple ways to receive weather
warnings.


* ADDITIONAL SOURCES OF INFORMATION:
- For information on appropriate preparations see ready.gov
- For information on creating an emergency plan see getagameplan.org
- For additional disaster preparedness information see redcross.org

-----------

illnesses.
properties.instruction:

shaded or air conditioned environments. Anyone overcome by heat

emergency! Call 9 1 1.

inches above 2500 feet along the Richardson Highway near Isabel
Pass, with heavier amounts above pass level. Northerly winds
gusting as high as 40 mph.

* WHERE...Eastern Alaska Range.

* WHEN...Until 4 AM AKDT Tuesday.

* IMPACTS...Travel could be difficult. Areas of blowing snow could
significantly reduce visibility.

precipitation and cloud cover so snowfall may continue through much
of the afternoon above 2500 feet.

call 5 1 1 for the latest road conditions.

properties.headline: Flood Watch issued August 31 at 2:34AM MST until September 1 at 12:00AM MST by NWS Flagstaff AZ
properties.description:
* WHAT...Flash flooding caused by excessive rainfall continues to be
possible.

* WHERE...All of northern and central Arizona.

* WHEN...Through this evening.

* IMPACTS...Flash flooding will be possible in creeks, normally dry
washes, swimming holes, and over recently burned areas. Raging
killer currents will be possible in side canyons and narrow slot
canyons. Low-water crossings may be flooded.

* ADDITIONAL DETAILS...
- Showers and thunderstorms are expected to continue this afternoon
and evening. With deep monsoonal moisture in place and already
saturated soils in some locations, an elevated risk of flash
flooding will be in place through Monday.
- Additional information is available at weather.gov/flagstaff.
properties.instruction:
Have a way to receive Flash Flood Warnings and be prepared to take
action should warnings be issued.

Consider changing your plans if you were going to hike, boat, or
paddleboard to a slot canyon or normally dry wash. If you do still
decide to recreate, check in at a nearby visitor center or ranger
station.

NWSheadline: FLOOD WATCH REMAINS IN EFFECT THROUGH THIS EVENING

properties.description:
The combination of hot temperatures and humidity levels will
produce heat index values between 105 and 110 degrees for several
hours this afternoon into this evening. A few locations may
briefly experience heat index values at or above 111 degrees.

If spending time outside, drink plenty of water, wear light
weight and light colored clothing, and take frequent breaks from
the heat. Young children and pets should never be left unattended
in vehicles.

properties.description:
* WHAT...Temperatures will be as low as 29 degrees on Tuesday will
result in frost formation.

* WHERE...Colder locations throughout the Anchorage Bowl and Lower
Matanuska Valley.

* WHEN...From 2 AM to 9 AM AKDT Tuesday.

* IMPACTS...Frost could harm sensitive outdoor vegetation. Sensitive
outdoor plants may be killed if left uncovered.

* ADDITIONAL DETAILS...Typically colder areas of Anchorage and
Matanuska Valley, such as Butte, Muldoon, Campbell Tract, and the
Eagle River Valley, are susceptible to below freezing temperatures
early Tuesday morning. Most areas of the Anchorage and the
Matanuska Valley will see temperatures in the 30s but remain above
freezing.
properties.instruction: Take steps now to protect tender plants from the cold.
